extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of military/naval history (and practitioners studying historical naval strategy)
extracted.subtask_description: A book-chapter style historical narrative describing naval and military operations, decisions, logistics, and strategy during the Spanish–American War. Aimed at explaining causes, conduct, and consequences of campaigns in a readable, educative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanying support vessels required
rubrics_metrics.description: Fighting vessels were totally unsupplied with that cloud of servers--colliers, mother ships, hospital ships, and scouts--which we now know must accompany a fleet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modern fleet needs a logistical ‘cloud’ of support ships for coal, repairs, medical care, and reconnaissance; absence of these severely limits operational reach and sustainability (merchant marine at low point could not fill need).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound professional training of personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: In personnel, however, the American Navy soon proved its overwhelming superiority, which was due not solely to innate ability but also to sound professional training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of crews and professional education (officers like Mahan, appointed War Board members) can outweigh nominal parity in ships or tonnage; professional institutions and training are decisive in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of concentration, not dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the navy were to accomplish all these purposes, it would have to work upon the principle of concentration and not dispersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To destroy an enemy fleet and secure objectives, forces should be concentrated for decisive action rather than spread thin guarding many points; concentration creates and maintains naval superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish control of the seas by destroying enemy fleet
rubrics_metrics.description: The fleet had performed its primary function: it had established its superiority and had obtained the control of the seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sea control (via decisive engagements and blockade) is foundational: protecting coast and commerce and enabling expeditionary forces depend on naval supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockade to sever enemy communications and supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuba must be cut off from Spain by blockade, and the seas must be made safe for the passage of the American Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A blockade is a strategic means to isolate an enemy possession, deny reinforcements/supplies, and enable land operations; it should be comprehensive and enforced with sufficient ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent political alliances with insurgents
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable, as far as possible, and consistent for your success and safety, not to have political alliances with the insurgents or any faction in the islands that would incur liability to maintain their cause in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical cooperation with local insurgents may be useful, but formal political entanglement risks long-term obligations; keep relations strictly instrumental and temporary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain operational secrecy from the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The navy was dogged by press dispatch boats which revealed its every move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press access and disclosure of movements can compromise operations; operational security is essential even under intense public and press interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance daring with technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Commodore Dewey belonged to that school of American naval officers who combine the spirit of Farragut's 'Damn the torpedoes' with a thorough knowledge of the latest scientific devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective commanders take bold risks but pair audacity with understanding of current technology and scientific developments; take precautions yet avoid paralysis by fear of the unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics (coal, supplies) constrain operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Schley began the blockade on the 28th of May, but stated that he could not continue long in position owing to lack of coal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of fuel, supplies, and coaling stations determines how long blockades and distant operations can be sustained; logistical planning must match operational ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of reconnaissance and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Lieutenant Victor Blue...boldly plunging into the Cuban wilderness to obtain information...and Lieutenant A. S. Rowan of the army, whose energy and initiative...are immortalized in Elbert Hubbard's 'Message to Garcia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate intelligence gathered by daring scouts is critical; individual initiative in overcoming obstacles yields strategic advantage despite risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper strength is deceptive; real efficiency matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ton for ton, gun for gun, it stood on fairly even terms with that of Spain...the fairly even balance of the two fleets...was entirely deceptive when it came to real efficiency in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raw metrics (tonnage, gun count) can mislead—training, crew quality, tactical doctrine, and leadership determine combat effectiveness more than nominal hardware parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialized blockade measures (e.g., sinking obstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and simpler expedient was to make the harbor mouth impassable...to sink the collier Merrimac...where, lying full length, she would completely prevent egress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineering/blocking operations (scuttling ships, mining, harbor obstruction) can be effective means of neutralizing an enemy fleet when direct assault or bombardment is impractical; these are delicate, risky tasks requiring volunteers and precise execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select strategic objectives based on enemy logistics and isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cervera found himself...at the extreme eastern end of Cuba in a port with no railroad connection with Havana...and totally unable to supply him with necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing theaters where the enemy is isolated, without rail or supply lines, increases chances of containment and victory; enemy choice of base can determine the direction of your expeditionary effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized planning via naval staff structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Congress had not provided for a general staff, he himself appointed a Naval War Board, which served many of the same purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dedicated planning body (war board/general staff) aids coordination and strategic decision-making; centralized staff can compensate for institutional gaps and improve operational coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance coastal defense, commerce protection, and offensive aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The first duty of the navy was to protect the American coast...The Naval War Board, however, had to remember that it must protect not only the coast but commerce also, and that the United States was at war not to defend herself but to attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naval strategy must weigh defensive tasks (coast and commerce protection) against offensive requirements (blockade, fleet engagements, enabling expeditionary forces); prioritize based on overall strategic aim rather than local panic.
